path.title: Product Management Fundamentals
path.subtitle: Make decisions that survive contact with engineering
path.summary: Most first-time PMs think the job is writing JIRA tickets and chairing standups. The job is actually translation and sequencing — taking a vague founder ask and turning it into a thing engineers can build, users can love, and sales can sell. By the end of this path you can scope a stakeholder request, run a real user interview, write a one-page PRD, prioritize a backlog, build a quarterly roadmap, ship a feature, and measure whether it worked.

skills.name: PM Mental Model
skills.description: Frame the PM job as translation plus sequencing rather than ticket-writing

skills.name: User Research
skills.description: Run interviews that surface real pain instead of polite agreement

skills.name: PRDs and Prioritization
skills.description: Write one-page specs and rank work using value, effort, and risk

skills.name: Roadmapping
skills.description: Build a now-next-later roadmap that aligns stakeholders without overpromising

skills.name: Launch and Measurement
skills.description: Run pre-mortems, ship features safely, and read post-launch metrics

skills.name: Product Judgment
skills.description: Apply tradeoff thinking across ambiguous, multi-stakeholder situations

assessment.title: Product Management Fundamentals Assessment
assessment.description: Tests whether you can apply PM judgment across scoping, user research, prioritization, roadmapping, and launch. Most questions have one defensible right answer; a few have two. Read carefully — the wrong answers are wrong on purpose.

questions.stem: Your CEO forwards an email from your biggest customer asking for a 'simple feature — just let admins export user data to Excel.' What is the right first move?

choices.label: Open a JIRA ticket and forward it to engineering with the customer email pasted in.
choices.explanation: Translation is the PM's job. The engineer needs the why and the constraints, not a forwarded thread.

choices.label: Reply to the CEO with the three-question scope test: who, what change in their day, what happens if we do nothing.
choices.explanation: The scope test exposes whether this is one feature, three features, or a workaround for a different missing feature.

choices.label: Schedule a one-hour requirements meeting with the customer and three engineers.
choices.explanation: Premature. You don't yet know if this is worth an engineer's hour, let alone four.

choices.label: Estimate it yourself and put it on next sprint.
choices.explanation: Estimating something you haven't scoped is how 'just an export' becomes a six-week saga.

questions.stem: Which of the following count as outcomes (not outputs)? Pick all that apply.

choices.label: Reduce time to first invoice from 4 days to under 1 day
choices.explanation: Measurable change in user behavior. Outcome.

choices.label: Ship the new invoicing module by Q3
choices.explanation: Output. Says nothing about whether anyone uses it.

choices.label: Increase weekly active admins from 38 percent to 55 percent
choices.explanation: Behavior change with a number. Outcome.

choices.label: Launch a redesigned dashboard
choices.explanation: A redesign is a thing you ship; whether it moves a metric is the outcome.

questions.stem: You're interviewing a user who says 'I would absolutely use a dark mode if you built one.' What is the highest-signal next question?

choices.label: Great — what shade of dark would you prefer?
choices.explanation: Designs the feature before you've validated the problem.

choices.label: Tell me about the last time the current screen actually hurt your eyes or your work.
choices.explanation: Past behavior beats hypothetical preference. If they can't recall a moment, the demand is theoretical.

choices.label: On a scale of 1 to 10, how likely are you to use it?
choices.explanation: Stated intent is a known liar. The 9 becomes a 2 at launch.

choices.label: Would you pay extra for it?
choices.explanation: Pricing questions in a discovery call get polite nonsense.

questions.stem: Why does the 'silence move' work in user interviews?

choices.label: It makes the interviewer look thoughtful and senior.
choices.explanation: Optics, not signal.

choices.label: After a user finishes their first answer, three to five seconds of silence pulls out the second, more honest answer.
choices.explanation: The first answer is the social-acceptable one. The second is closer to the truth.

choices.label: It saves time on calls.
choices.explanation: It actually slows the call down on purpose.

choices.label: It avoids leading questions.
choices.explanation: Silence is unrelated to leading. The point is depth, not bias.

questions.stem: Which of these are red flags in a user interview transcript? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Every answer starts with 'I would' or 'I might'
choices.explanation: Hypotheticals. You want stories about what they actually did.

choices.label: User describes the last time they hit the problem with a date and a workaround
choices.explanation: Gold. This is exactly what you want.

choices.label: User suggests a specific UI solution within 2 minutes of the call starting
choices.explanation: Solution mode. Reset to the underlying job.

choices.label: User pauses for 4 seconds before answering a question
choices.explanation: Pauses are signal, not noise. They mean the user is actually thinking.

questions.stem: A PRD is best understood as:

choices.label: A specification document for the engineers
choices.explanation: Too narrow. Engineers are one audience. Sales, support, and future-you also read it.

choices.label: A contract with future-you about what 'done' means
choices.explanation: The PRD's job is to make 'done' unambiguous before the work starts. Future-you is the toughest stakeholder.

choices.label: A marketing brief for launch
choices.explanation: That's a launch plan, not a PRD.

choices.label: A wireframe with notes
choices.explanation: Wireframes are a tool inside a PRD, not the PRD itself.

questions.stem: You're using RICE to score 6 potential features. Feature A scores 800, feature B scores 720. Both have similar effort. The CEO is pushing for B. What does the framework actually tell you to do?

choices.label: Build A, the higher score wins.
choices.explanation: RICE is decision support, not a decision oracle. An 11 percent gap is within the noise of your own confidence numbers.

choices.label: Build B, the CEO's gut is the tiebreaker.
choices.explanation: Defaulting to HiPPO (highest-paid person's opinion) skips the actual question: what does the CEO know that your inputs missed?

choices.label: Treat the scores as a tie and decide on a non-RICE factor — strategic fit, dependency unlock, or learning value.
choices.explanation: When scores are within ~15 percent, the model is signalling 'these are equivalent; use judgment.' That's the point of decision support.

choices.label: Re-run RICE with stricter inputs until one wins.
choices.explanation: Tweaking the inputs to get the answer you want is how RICE becomes theatre.

questions.stem: What does the 'cut, don't compromise' rule mean in practice?

choices.label: Never reduce scope; ship the full thing or ship nothing.
choices.explanation: The opposite. The rule is about cutting features, not refusing to cut.

choices.label: When you must reduce scope, drop entire features rather than building half of every feature.
choices.explanation: Three good features beat six half-features. Half-features become support tickets.

choices.label: Compromise on quality before scope.
choices.explanation: Backwards. Scope flexes; quality doesn't.

choices.label: Cut deadlines, never features.
choices.explanation: Sometimes the deadline matters more than the scope. The rule is about how to cut, not whether to.

questions.stem: Why is a roadmap longer than one quarter mostly fiction?

choices.label: Engineers can't estimate that far out.
choices.explanation: True but secondary. Even with perfect estimates, the inputs change.

choices.label: User behavior, competitor moves, and your own learnings invalidate the assumptions every 6 to 10 weeks.
choices.explanation: A roadmap is built on assumptions about the world. The world's update frequency is faster than two quarters.

choices.label: Stakeholders forget what was on it.
choices.explanation: They don't, actually. They remember it word for word and quote it back at you.

choices.label: Deadlines slip.
choices.explanation: Slipping is symptom, not cause.

questions.stem: Which of these are valid uses of a roadmap? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Telling the same coherent story to sales, engineering, and the board
choices.explanation: Alignment is the primary job. One story, three audiences.

choices.label: Committing to ship feature X by month Y to a customer
choices.explanation: That's a contract. Roadmaps are not contracts.

choices.label: Showing the why behind your sequencing — not just the what
choices.explanation: If a roadmap is just a list of features, you've built a backlog, not a roadmap.

choices.label: Listing every JIRA ticket for the next year
choices.explanation: That's a backlog dump. Nobody reads past row 7.

questions.stem: Sales asks you to commit a feature to a prospect to close a deal. The feature isn't on the roadmap. What's the strongest first response?

choices.label: Yes, we can ship it next sprint.
choices.explanation: Whiplashed roadmap. Every other customer's feature just got bumped.

choices.label: No, it's not on the roadmap.
choices.explanation: Right answer, wrong delivery. Sales loses a deal and respect for product.

choices.label: Help me understand the deal — size, timing, and which 5 other customers want this. I'll come back tomorrow with a yes, no, or a swap.
choices.explanation: The polite no template. You're not refusing; you're moving to evidence-based decision.

choices.label: Add it to the backlog and move on.
choices.explanation: Hiding from a decision. Sales reads silence as agreement.

choices.label: A retrospective held before the project starts.
choices.explanation: Close, but a retrospective is about what happened. A pre-mortem is about what could go wrong.

choices.label: An exercise where the team imagines the launch failed and lists the most likely reasons, before shipping.
choices.explanation: Surfacing failure modes early, while they're cheap to fix, instead of later in the postmortem when they're expensive.

choices.label: A risk register filled in by engineering management.
choices.explanation: Risk registers are bureaucratic; pre-mortems are imaginative.

choices.label: A QA test plan.
choices.explanation: QA verifies known things; pre-mortem surfaces unknown things.

questions.stem: On day 7 after launch, which signals are most worth your attention? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Activation rate of users who reached the new feature
choices.explanation: Tells you if the feature is even discoverable and usable.

choices.label: Total page views on the launch blog post
choices.explanation: Vanity. Tells you about marketing, not product.

choices.label: Day-7 retention of users who tried the feature vs those who didn't
choices.explanation: The clearest signal that the feature added real value, not novelty.

choices.label: Number of internal Slack messages from sales about the launch
choices.explanation: Internal noise. Useful for politics, not for product decisions.

questions.stem: Your B2B SaaS has DAU/MAU of 0.18. Industry good is 0.4. Your CEO says 'great, lots of room to grow.' What's the more accurate read?

choices.label: The CEO is right; we're underpenetrated.
choices.explanation: DAU/MAU below 0.2 in B2B usually means you're a 'logged-in occasionally' tool, not a daily habit.

choices.label: We have an engagement problem, not a growth problem; new users won't fix what existing users won't do.
choices.explanation: Pouring users into a leaky bucket is the most expensive mistake B2B SaaS makes.

choices.label: DAU/MAU doesn't matter for B2B.
choices.explanation: It matters; the threshold is just lower than consumer.

choices.label: Switch to MAU/QAU.
choices.explanation: Hiding the problem behind a softer denominator.

questions.stem: You shipped a feature. Activation is good (60 percent of users tried it), but day-30 retention of those users is 8 percent lower than non-users. What does this most likely mean?

choices.label: The feature is great; users just need more education.
choices.explanation: When usage actively predicts churn, the feature is anti-value, not under-marketed.

choices.label: The feature is creating friction or false expectations; investigate before promoting it further.
choices.explanation: Negative correlation with retention is a stop signal. Find out why before you spend on adoption.

choices.label: Day-30 retention is too noisy to read; ignore it.
choices.explanation: 8 percentage points on a 30-day cohort is well above noise for most products.

choices.label: Retention will recover at day 60.
choices.explanation: Hope is not a plan.

questions.stem: An engineer says 'this will take 2 weeks.' Translated through PM judgment, the realistic ship date is roughly:

choices.label: 2 weeks
choices.explanation: Pure estimate, no buffer for the unknowns. You will be wrong.

choices.label: 3 to 4 weeks once you account for review, QA, edge cases, and one mid-project surprise
choices.explanation: The 1.5-2x rule on engineering estimates is empirical across most teams. Plan for it.

choices.label: 8 weeks; engineers always lie
choices.explanation: Cynicism, not judgment. Most estimates are honest, just optimistic about smooth paths.

choices.label: 1 week; engineers pad
choices.explanation: The opposite assumption is even worse. You'll commit to a date you cannot hit.

questions.stem: Which of these are the PM's job? Select all that apply.

choices.label: Deciding what NOT to build
choices.explanation: Saying no, with reasons, is more of the job than saying yes.

choices.label: Writing the production code
choices.explanation: If the PM is writing code, the engineering team is missing a person.

choices.label: Translating between users, engineers, sales, and leadership so each understands the others
choices.explanation: The translator role is the load-bearing wall of the job.

choices.label: Approving design pixel-by-pixel
choices.explanation: That's design's craft; PM weighs in on flow and tradeoffs, not pixels.

project.title: Capstone: The Sales-Forwarded Feature Request
project.prompt:
You are six weeks into your first PM role at **Tarakash**, a Bengaluru-based B2B SaaS that sells warehouse-management software to mid-market 3PL companies. Your VP-Sales, Vivek, forwards you this email at 9:47 PM:

> *Hey, urgent. Acme Logistics (₹38L ARR, second-largest customer, renewal in 11 weeks) wants 'a proper Excel export from the inventory dashboard, with filters and scheduling, plus a Hindi version of the UI for their warehouse staff in Lucknow.' Their COO said this is a 'must-have' for renewal. Can we get this on next sprint? — V*

It is Tuesday. Renewal conversations start in 4 weeks. Engineering is mid-way through a long-promised reliability sprint. The next planning meeting is Friday morning.

Write a **one-page response** (around 400-500 words) that you would send back to Vivek before the planning meeting. Your response must:

1. Apply the **3-question scope test** to break the request into separable pieces.
2. State which pieces (if any) you would commit to, which you would defer, and which you would refuse — with a reason for each.
3. Identify the **one user-research move** you would make in the next 48 hours to de-risk the decision.
4. Propose a **concrete next step** for Vivek, the engineering lead, and the customer — each with an owner and a date.

You may use bullet lists. Do not write a PRD. Do not promise dates you cannot defend. Write in the tone you would actually send to a VP at 10 PM — direct, calm, no jargon padding.

levels.label: Decomposes the request into distinct pieces; states a clear yes/no/defer for each with a reason; the VP could forward this email to the CEO without rewriting it
Identifies most pieces and takes a position, but reasoning is partially missing or buried
Treats the request as one undifferentiated ask, or hedges every position
Acknowledges Vivek's renewal pressure and the customer's underlying job; engages the engineering reliability sprint as a real constraint, not as an excuse
Considers one stakeholder well but dismisses or ignores another
Treats stakeholders as obstacles, or copy-pastes a 'no' template without context
Proposes a specific user-research move within 48 hours, names owners and dates for each next action, and gives Vivek something to send the customer by Friday
Has next steps but they are vague on owners, dates, or sequencing
Ends with 'let's discuss in the meeting' or no actionable steps

credential.title: Product Management Fundamentals
credential.description: Holder can scope a stakeholder ask, run a real user interview, write a one-page PRD, prioritize a backlog using RICE or value-vs-effort, build a now-next-later roadmap, and read post-launch metrics with judgment.
